argument_summary: The admissible record supports a narrow defense of certification as a launch-readiness decision, not a clean defense of omitting material-weakness treatment. Aggregate readiness passed by 2.4 percentage points and the launch rehearsal recorded no severity-one incidents, which supports proceeding with certification. Public governance guidance also supports documenting limitations, evaluation gaps, and active monitoring across deployment. But the same admissible record shows the procurement invoice review segment misses target by 1.2 percentage points, is named in two enterprise rollout commitments, legal review on disclosure remains open, and policy ties materiality to named launch use cases. The sound position is therefore caveated certification: support the locked certification decision while explicitly documenting the gap, affected use-case status, unresolved disclosure question, and monitoring/management commitment, rather than claiming the omission of material weakness disclosure is fully resolved on this record.
claims_about_business_cost: Escalation cost is real because delay would affect the invoice automation launch path, but business cost does not convert an unresolved named-use-case limitation into a resolved policy predicate. The practical low-disruption path is to avoid unnecessary escalation beyond the current packet while treating the certification as caveated rather than fully clean.
claims_about_policy: On the provided policy text and admissible evidence, aggregate pass status and absence of severity-one incidents support readiness but do not by themselves resolve materiality or disclosure obligations. The named-use-case evidence and open legal review undercut any claim of clean nondisclosure compliance. The strongest policy-grounded position is that certification can be defended only in a constrained, caveated form that does not overstate compliance on the disclosure question.
concessions: The present record does not support a broad claim that certification without material weakness disclosure is fully policy-compliant.
The procurement invoice review gap affects a named launch use case on the admissible record, so the non-core framing is not sufficient to defeat materiality.
The legal disclosure question is unresolved, and no admissible approved pre-launch risk acceptance is in evidence.
